newsitem.title: USA: Man extradited to U.S. for giant insurance fraud.
newsitem.headline: Man extradited to U.S. for giant insurance fraud.

text.p: The man accused of masterminding one of the biggest insurance frauds in U.S. history was extradited from Switzerland to face trial in federal court, U.S. officials said on Friday.
Martin Bramson, 51, was due to arrive at Dulles International Airport in Virginia late in the day in the custody of U.S. marshals, ending a 2-1/2 year fight against extradition.
An official with the U.S. Attorney's Office said Bramson would appear at a preliminary hearing in U.S. District Court in Baltimore on Monday.

Prosecutors allege that Bramson, his brother Leonard and father Norman swindled American doctors in 48 states out of $20 million by offering bargain-rate malpractice and other insurance policies that turned out to be bogus.

The Bramsons, who had received training in medicine and the law, set up a network of insurance companies and accepted millions in premium payments through a Maryland post office box. But the companies were not licensed in each state and had not complied with laws requiring millions of dollars in reserves to protect policyholders.

The family refused to pay out on claims, while funnelling premiums into more than 600 bank accounts in such far-flung locales as Luxembourg, Panama, Israel, Germany, Guam and the Netherlands, officials said.
Prosecutors hope to retrieve that money, plus $3.2 million in gold and Swiss francs which Bramson had with him when he was arrested in the tiny European nation of Liechtenstein in 1995.

Bramson, a former pharmacist with a law degree, was turned over to Swiss authorities and has been in jail in Switzerland since last fall. He lost his final extradition appeal to the Swiss Supreme Court on July 16.
Now, he could face 15-30 years in prison, if convicted on charges that include money laundering, wire fraud and mail fraud.
Leonard and Norman Bramson were sentenced to federal prison terms while Martin lived as an international fugitive after fleeing house arrest in 1991.
At a 1994 sentencing hearing, an attorney for Leonard Bramson described Martin as the larger culprit in the scheme.
